description: What stands between an agent's edit and a commit.
text: Gate The gate is : one offline command that names every problem in a library in one pass and changes nothing. It passes only when no check reports an error. Every skill runs the gate before it commits, and continuous integration runs the same command. So a broken link, an orphan, a missing field, a placeholder left in a page or an edited record never reaches a reader. It reads the files as they are and compares the records with git. It never fixes anything: it names each problem with its file and its check, and the skill that made the edit fixes it. An edit passes through folio check before it can be committed the edit by a skill folio check links each genre's card lifecycles against git maps and orphans ids and indices open questions' quotes the packs' rules one pass, changes nothing commit no error every problem named at once fix, then run it again The gate sits between the edit and the commit. It does not stop at the first problem: it reports them all, so one round of fixes is usually enough. What each kind of check catches Every check has a name, listed in the checks specification, and every problem the gate reports carries the file, the severity, the check's name and what is wrong. Pick a kind of check to see one problem it catches, as the gate reports it. The files in the lines are examples. Linksbroken-link The cardlocation, fields, status Lifecyclepermanent, frozen Mapsorphan, home-maps Ids and indicesunique-id, index-current Commentsstale-quote Pack rulesuncited-number and more Papersbib, figures Links Every link and citation resolves, the way the exported site serves it: an , an id in backticks, a field of type id, a . A renamed page whose old links were not rewritten shows up here. content/notes/tiling.html: error broken-link: `/content/concepts/softmx/` resolves to nothing The card Each document meets its genre's card: it sits at the card's path, carries the core metadata and the card's fields, uses one of the card's status words, keeps the parts the machine reads (a concept's definition, a map's rows), and leaves no placeholder behind. location fields status placeholder require cites defined_once content/concepts/softmax/index.html: error status: status `done` is not one of draft, live, historical, retired Lifecycle A permanent document is compared with its first commit, and a frozen one with the commit that froze it. An edit to a committed journal entry or result is caught here, however small. content/journal/2026/2026-10-02-switched-the-kernel.md: error permanent: a permanent document has changed since its first commit; restore it and record the change in a new document Maps Every document except a journal entry is on a map, or linked from a map or from a document on one. Every map the charter names as a home map exists and is not a draft. content/notes/loose-idea.html: error orphan: is on no map; add it with `folio map add <map> <doc>` Ids and indices Ids are unique across the library whatever the genre, compared without regard to case, and a record id is never reused. The generated indices in match what would write. content/notes/attention.html: error unique-id: id `attention` is also the id of content/entries/attention/index.html; ids are unique across the library, whatever their case Comments An open question still quotes text that is on its page. An edit that rewrote the passage a reader asked about fails the gate until the question is answered. content/entries/attention-cost/index.html: error stale-quote: open thread t3 quotes text no longer on the page: `costs grow with the square of the context` Pack rules A pack that is switched on adds rule checks across the whole library. The lab pack's asks that a number shaped like a measurement cite a result in the same sentence; flags a revised page that cites a superseded result. The knowledge-base pack's asks that a source's identifiers be verified. content/notes/check-speed.html: warning uncited-number: a number looks like a measurement and cites no result in its sentence, item or row; cite the result, or wrap it as not measured Papers In a paper, every resolves, every key is in the library's bibliography, and every figure comes from . bib figures broken-link content/papers/attention/main.tex: error bib: has a bibliography of its own; use assets/refs.bib Error, warning or off Each check has a default severity. The charter changes it by the check's name, under , so a library decides how strict it is without touching a card. error Fails the gate. The skill does not commit until it is fixed. warning Reported in the same pass, and the gate still passes. A new lab library starts here. off Not run. A library that has a reason to skip a check says so in its charter, where every reader can see it. The trap: expecting the gate to judge quality. It checks what can be checked: shape, links, fields, lifecycles, indices. Whether an argument holds is judged by the agent following its genre's card, and by the owner. Related The charter sets each check to error, warning or off. A pack adds rule checks of its own. Every skill that changes a document ends here. What it holds to git The gate is why a permanent record stays permanent: the promise is compared with history on every run, not hoped for.
title: Gate

description: Why every document in a library has a fixed job, voice, format and set of checks.
text: Genre A genre is a kind of document, such as a concept, a note or a result. It fixes the document's job, its reader, its voice, its format, where it lives, which metadata it carries, how it may change over time, and which checks it must pass. An agent writing a document reads its genre's card first, every time. So two documents of one genre read as if one author wrote them, and the gate can check what each genre promises. Voice is never set per document. A genre gives structure and voice, never form. How an HTML page looks is its author's, on a free canvas: the card fixes what the page is, and the page decides how to show it. What a card fixes, and what it leaves to the page Each row below is something a card decides. The last row is the one thing it does not. Pick a genre to read its card down the column. Read the card of concept journal result map Jobwhat it is for concept Defines one term, once, so every other document can link to it. journal Records one thing that happened or was decided, on its date. result Holds one measured number, with its baseline, bound, evidence and the command that re-derives it. map A front door over part of the library, in the order to read it. Readerwho opens it concept Someone who met the term elsewhere, often reading only the popover. journal The owner or a collaborator, later, reconstructing a decision. result Anyone about to cite the number, and anyone who doubts it. map Someone arriving cold. Voicehow it sounds concept Impersonal, present tense, timeless. journal Terse. Past tense for what happened, present for what holds from now on. result Terse and numeric. The bound sits beside the number. map Opinionated and brief. Format and placeone format, one path concept HTML, at . journal Markdown, at . result Markdown, at , from the lab pack. map HTML, at . Metadatafields beyond the core concept None. journal , required; and , optional. result , , , , , , ; when it replaces one. map None. Lifecyclehow it may change concept Revised in place: draft, live, historical, retired. journal Permanent once committed. Its status is derived. result Permanent once committed: live, superseded or retracted, derived from other documents. map Revised in place: draft, live, historical, retired. Checkswhat the gate holds it to concept A definition is present, cites nothing, and is the only one of its term. journal Its kind is one the library accepts; a word cap; unchanged since its first commit. result A section; a word cap; every field present; unchanged since its first commit. map Its rows are present, and it is itself on a map. Left to the page Formlayout, figures, controls concept The author's, on the canvas. This page is one example. journal A Markdown record: always set in the reading column. result A Markdown record: always set in the reading column. map The author's, on the canvas, around its rows. Read down any column: every row above the line has a value, and it is the card's, not the author's. Only the last row changes from page to page. Where a genre comes from A genre is a folder holding its card and a skeleton. folio looks for it in three places, and the first one found wins. An override in the library holds only what it changes, so the card underneath still applies and folio's upgrades flow in. First The library's own : an override, a variant or a genre of its own. Then A pack switched on in the charter, which adds genres under names no other genre uses. Last folio's core: concept, note, entry, map, guide, project, journal and paper. A variant, for a second audience A genre can extend another. The variant inherits everything and overrides only what it states: usually the voice, the reader and the limits. A paper for a workshop extends the paper. A document changes genre only by promotion, as when a note that grew sections becomes an entry, and promotion keeps its id, links, comments and dates. The trap: treating a genre as a template. The skeleton is the smallest part of it. The card also says what the document is for and what it must never do, and most of that is judged by the agent, not checked. Related The core has eight genres. A pack adds more, and a library can override a genre or add a variant for a second audience. Where it is checked The gate runs each card's checks on every document of its genre. Whether a page does its job well is left to the agent and the owner.
title: Genre

description: Where a library keeps the dated record of what happened and why.
text: Journal The journal is a library's dated record of what happened and what was decided. Each entry is its own short Markdown file with a date, an optional kind, and the ids of the documents it is about. Documents say what is true now; the journal says when it changed and why. An entry shows on every document it names, and the shell renders all entries as one timeline that filters by kind, tag, date or document. One entry file shows on the timeline and on each document it is about {date}-{slug}.md date: … kind: decision about: [journal] a few terse lines the timeline newest first, filtered each page it names in the page panel The entry is written once. The shell places it on the timeline and on every document in its , so nobody keeps a "history" section by hand. This library's journal, one file each These are the entries in this library's own journal, grouped by day. Each is its own file, and each links to its page. Filter by kind, as the timeline does. Every entry decision lock no kind 2026-10-04 Library set up 2026-10-04-library-set-up.md decision about The library shares the repository's skills 2026-10-04-the-library-shares-the-repository-s-skills.md decision about Home maps set 2026-10-04-home-maps-set.md decision about Specifications stay outside the library 2026-10-04-specifications-stay-outside-the-library.md decision about Comments are committed by the server, as the commenter 2026-10-04-comments-are-committed-by-the-server.md decision about Ingested As We May Think 2026-10-04-ingested-as-we-may-think.md no kind about Locked the check-time protocol 2026-10-04-locked-the-check-time-protocol.md lock about Recorded R-1 2026-10-04-recorded-r-1.md no kind about Recorded R-2 2026-10-04-recorded-r-2.md no kind about Added How folio is built as a home map 2026-10-04-added-how-folio-is-built-as.md decision about 2026-10-03 One journal entry per file 2026-10-03-one-journal-entry-per-file.md decision about Metadata holds every fact the engine reads 2026-10-03-metadata-holds-every-fact-the-engine.md decision about Paper versions are snapshots 2026-10-03-paper-versions-are-snapshots.md decision about Every entry is a separate file under . Within a day the order here is not the order of events; the date is. The entry about on the first day is the decision that gave the journal this shape. Why one file per entry A single log file would be shorter to read in an editor. One file per entry buys three things the log cannot give. One file per entry Two agents writing at once never touch the same file, so they never conflict. Every entry has its own address, so it can be linked and searched on its own. Every entry is a permanent record , and the gate compares each file with its first commit. One log file Every new entry edits the same file, so concurrent writers collide. An entry is a heading inside a long page, not a document, so nothing can name it in or show it on a page. The file changes every day, so no line in it can be held to its first commit. Kinds A kind is optional. The shell filters by it, and two kinds change what readers see on the document they name. Kinds are an open set: the core has four, a pack adds its own while it is on, and the charter adds more under . The core's four decision A choice that binds later work. lesson Something learned the hard way. correction Says a document was wrong and what is true instead; shows as a banner on it. retraction Withdraws a record, which is then marked retracted. Added here by the lab pack , , , and . An entry with no kind is a plain event, such as a source ingested or a result recorded. The trap: writing a decision only into the page it changed. The page will be revised again and the reason lost. The decision goes in the journal, about that page. Related Every entry is a permanent record , and the only document no map needs to list. Who writes it Every skill that makes a decision records it as a new entry with , which writes a new file and never edits an existing one.
title: Journal

description: The unit folio works on: where it lives and what it holds.
text: Library A library is a folder holding a charter, a folder of linked documents, an folder, and the generated indices in . It can be a project's folder, a notes folder, or a whole repository. Everything folio does is scoped to one library. The folder on the right is the whole of one. Every document is under , one folder per genre ; nothing outside it is a document. Pick a writer to see which folders it owns. No folder has two. Every folder The charter Documents Its own genres Generated folio.yaml The charter: name, purpose, reader, voice, packs, home maps, check severities. content/ Every document, one folder per genre, the journal included. index.html The home page, the map named . concepts/<slug>/ A concept, with its files beside it. journal/<yyyy>/ One Markdown file per entry. maps/, notes/, … Each other genre's folder, as its card names it. assets/ What documents cite but are not documents. figures/ Figure sources and their rendered files. refs.bib The library's one bibliography. data/ Datasets that documents cite. genres/<name>/ This library's overrides, variants and genres of its own. workflows/<name>.md This library's own workflows. packs/<name>/ This library's own packs. .folio/ The generated indices, committed, and checked current by the gate. catalog.json Every document's metadata, map rows and topics. backlinks.json, search.json What cites what, and the search index. nav.json, journal.json, cards.json Guide navigation, the timeline and the flashcards. redirects.json The one file here that is state: old addresses, written by moves. The charter says what the library is. Only the set-up and configure skills write it, and every change is shown as a diff and recorded in the journal. Documents are written through the skills, and every one goes through write, its genre's card and the gate. Assets are committed with the documents that cite them. Its own genres, workflows and packs are added and changed by the configure skill. Each is found before a pack's or the core's of the same name. Generated files are written by and never by hand. is written by , and . The coloured edge on each row is its writer. The script only dims the rows of the other writers; every description is on the page either way. Where a library sits A library is wherever a is. One project can hold more than one. When a library sits inside a larger project, the charter's names the project root, and a path a document gives to something outside the library, such as a result's evidence, resolves from there. A project's docs/ The library beside the code it documents. This library is one: folio's own , with pointing at the repository. A notes folder A personal library of concepts, notes and readings, inside whatever repository holds it. A whole repository The repository is the library, and its root holds the charter. One library, one scope The gate checks one library. The site exports one library. Ids are unique within one library, whatever the genre. Search covers one library, and a charter can list others to search alongside its own. The trap: reading the library as a website. The pages are plain HTML and Markdown in git, readable with no build step. The site is one view of them, written by export. Related Every document in a library has a genre , and readers enter through its maps . What changes it Every change goes through one of the seven skills , which call the command and end at the gate.
title: Library

description: How a reader finds their way into a library without a folder tree.
text: Map A map is a document that lists other documents in the order to read them, each row with an optional one-line reason to follow it. The maps the charter names as home maps are the library's topics, drawn on its home page. A library has no folder tree for a reader to browse; folders follow genres, not subjects. Maps are the structure instead. A document can sit on several maps, and a map can list other maps, so one library can have as many front doors as it needs. What falls under a topic follows from the maps. Nothing on a document declares its topic. How the maps nest, in this library The home page is a map. The charter names four home maps under , and each lists its rows in reading order. Pick a topic to focus on it, as the Focus control in the top bar does: what falls under it stays lit, wherever it sits. Focus Whole library Using folio Concepts Reference How folio is built Home page The map named , under every topic. The shell draws a card for each home map, in the charter's order. Using folio Getting started guide folio project · on two maps Why metadata comes first entry One fact, one home entry How corrections work entry As We May Think reading As We May Think source Q-1 question · on two maps Concepts Library concept Genre concept Map concept Skill concept Pack concept Gate concept Journal concept Permanent record concept Reference The folio modela spec, linked outside the library The genre formata spec, linked outside the library The checksa spec, linked outside the library The folio commanda spec, linked outside the library The pack formata spec, linked outside the library The skill formata spec, linked outside the library The shell's componentslinked outside the library How folio is built folio project · on two maps Q-1 question · on two maps check-time protocol R-1 result R-2 result Using folio. The guide, the project, three entries, a source with its reading, and the open question. The project and the question are lit on How folio is built too: a document is on every map that lists it. Concepts. The eight concepts. A concept is filed under no topic of its own: it also falls under every topic whose documents link it, so a focus on Using folio still reaches the concepts its entries use. Reference. The specifications. They stay Markdown files outside the library, so this map links them by their addresses on GitHub, and they fall under no topic. How folio is built. The lab records: the question, the protocol that tests it, and the two results. The project and the question are shared with Using folio. The tree is drawn from this library's own maps. Rows that sit on two maps say so; with a topic in focus, they stay lit on both. Maps, not folders Folders follow genres Every concept is under , every entry under . That tells the engine what a file is. It tells a reader nothing about where to start on a subject. Maps follow subjects A map picks documents of any genre, puts them in order, and says why each is worth following from here. The same document can be on a map for newcomers and on a map for one project. What one row holds A link To the document. The shell draws the link's text from the document's title, so a renamed document reads right on every map. A reason, optional One line on why to follow it from this map. Without one, the shell shows the document's description. A place Its order and its group heading, which the map keeps as written. The trap: using tags as structure. Tags are facets for filtering. A reader arriving cold needs an order and a reason, and only a map gives them. Related The gate checks that every document except a journal entry is reachable from a map. Who keeps them The write skill puts each new document on a map in the same change. The organise skill moves, merges and splits maps with every link kept.
title: Map

description: How a library gains genres and workflows for one kind of work.
text: Pack A pack is a named set of genres, workflows, library-wide rules and journal kinds for one kind of work. Switching it on in the charter adds them to the whole library and rewrites nothing. The core genres suit any library. A pack adds what one kind of work needs: the knowledge-base pack keeps sources and readings apart, and the lab pack gives every measured number one home. Several packs on at once still make one library, with one search and one graph. Layers over the core folio ships two packs. This library has both on. Switch each off and on, and watch what the library offers for new work. The core stays, and so do the skills on top. Switched on knowledge-base lab The seven skills the same in every setting Read The charter, every genre and every workflow that is on, each time they start. Never change A pack brings no skill. The run skill follows its workflows; write follows its cards. lab measured work on off Genres question, protocol, result, claim, report Workflows record-a-result, write-a-report Rules , Journal kinds lock, run, kill, instrument, pivot knowledge-base reading and learning on off Genres source, reading, survey Workflows ingest, quiz Rules Journal kinds None of its own. core always there Genres concept, note, entry, map, guide, project, journal, paper Workflows None. A library adds its own. Rules The gate checks only. No library-wide rule. Journal kinds decision, lesson, correction, retraction Off hides a pack's genres and workflows from new work. Documents already written in its genres stay valid, and its rules stop running. Each pack sits on the core without changing it: a pack's genres have names no other genre uses, and a pack never redefines a core genre. What switching one on does It adds Its genres, workflows, rules and journal kinds, to the whole library at once. The charter lists it under , and the configure skill records the change in the journal. It rewrites nothing No existing document is changed. A pack's rules can flag documents written before it was on, such as a number with no result to cite; the organise skill proposes the fixes. Where packs come from Shipped with folio knowledge-base and lab. The library's own In its folder. gathers library genres and workflows into one. A git repository Pinned in the charter by its address and a commit. The trap: expecting a pack to bring new skills. A pack is data only. The same skills read its genres and follow its workflows, so a new pack never needs a new skill. Related Each pack adds genres under names no other genre uses; it never redefines a core one. Its rules at the gate A pack's rules are checks the gate runs across the whole library while the pack is on. A library's own pack can only combine checks the gate already has.
title: Pack

description: Why some documents are never edited once committed, and how they still change status.
text: Permanent record A permanent record is a document whose genre declares it is never edited once committed, such as a journal entry or a result. It writes no status of its own; its status is derived from the documents that point back to it. A citation of a permanent record always shows what was cited, because the record cannot change under it. The gate compares each one with its first commit, so the promise is checked, not hoped for. The old record stays as committed; arrows from newer documents set its status R-1 committed once, never edited R-2 supersedes: R-1 journal entry kind: retraction names it or retracts it Nothing writes to the old record. Its status follows from the documents that point back at it: a newer record that names it in , or a journal entry that retracts it. One record, three states, no edits The record below is the same file in every state. Pick what happens to it, and see what the shell draws on its page. Only the status and the banner change, and both come from other documents. Nothing yet A newer result supersedes it A journal entry retracts it With scripts off, every state is described here. A record that nothing points back at is live . A newer record that names it in makes it superseded . A journal entry of kind about it makes it retracted . Live. Nothing points back at it. Every citation shows it as it was committed, and the shell draws no banner. Superseded. A newer result names it in its field. The old result keeps its address, so old citations still show what they cited, and a banner links the newer one. Retracted. A journal entry of kind names it in . The record stays readable, marked retracted, with a banner linking the entry that says why. Result · R-1 The gate's running time on this library, as first measured live superseded retracted Superseded. A newer result replaces this one; follow its link for the current number. Retracted. A journal entry withdraws this result and says why. The body is exactly as it was committed, in every state. The gate compares this file with its first commit. Permanent, frozen and revised Permanent Never edited once committed. A journal entry and a result. Its status is derived, never written. Frozen Edited freely until it reaches a state such as , then never again, except a status change to one of its card's exits. A protocol and a report. Revised Edited in place, and always current. Concepts, entries, maps and the rest of the pages. The trap: thinking permanent means it can never be wrong. It can be wrong, and the library says so: a newer record supersedes it, or a journal entry retracts or corrects it, and a banner on the record links the correction. What never happens is a quiet edit. Related The journal is made of permanent entries, one file each. The gate holds every permanent and frozen document to its history in git. The long form How a correction reaches every page that cited the old record is in How corrections work .
title: Permanent record

description: How an agent knows what to do with a library, step by step.
text: Skill A skill is a written procedure a coding agent follows to change a library: when to use it, its rules, its steps, when to stop, and when it is done. folio ships seven: set-up, configure, write, organise, address, publish and run. The person using folio talks to their agent in plain words, and the agent picks the matching skill. The skills call the command the way an agent calls git, so the person never needs to learn it. The set is fixed. What is specific to a kind of document lives in its genre's card, and what is specific to a procedure lives in a workflow, so neither needs a skill of its own. Seven skills around one command Every skill acts on the library through the same command. Pick a command to see which skills call it. Every skill The seven skills, each joined to the folio command in the middle folio the command set-up configure write organise address publish run : every skill. A change is done only when the gate passes. : six of the seven. Each records a decision as a new entry; address answers comments instead. : write alone. Every document any skill produces goes through write. : write, which puts a new document on a map, and organise, which keeps the maps current. : organise alone, with and , so a move keeps every link, comment and date. : address answers threads, write reads them and leaves flags, organise checks them before a move. : set-up and configure, the only two skills that write the charter. : publish alone, after the gate. set-up Installs a library once: the charter, the home page, the first journal entry. configure Changes the charter: packs, home maps, genres, variants, workflows. write Adds or revises any document, in its genre's voice, and puts it on a map. organise Moves, merges, promotes and retires, with every link kept; runs health passes. address Answers the comments readers left, on the page each was left on. publish Exports the static site, and builds and freezes papers. run Follows a workflow step by step; every document it makes goes through write. Each card lists the main commands its skill names, without the prefix. The command is shared; what differs between skills is which calls they make and in what order. Who talks to whom The person Asks in plain words: "add a concept for this", "tidy the maps". The agent Matches the words to a skill by its description, and reads it. The skill Its steps, rules and stops, followed in order. folio The command the skill calls, ending at the gate . Every skill starts the same way This is why a new genre, workflow or pack never needs a new skill: each one reads what the library offers before it acts. Find the library: the nearest . Read the charter. List the genres and workflows available, from the library, its packs and the core. Read the card for the genre in hand. The trap: thinking a new kind of document needs a new skill. Every skill starts by reading the charter, the genres and the workflows, so it already knows what a new genre or pack adds. Related Every skill that changes a document ends at the gate , then commits exactly the files it touched. Where they live The skills are installed in a library's , for any coding agent that reads that folder.
title: Skill

description: How a library corrects a document it may not edit, and what a reader sees, for anyone keeping records.
text: A record that was wrong is never edited. A new document points back at it, and the engine shows the correction on the record itself, so old citations keep showing what they cited and every reader of the record sees what changed. The argument runs in four steps: which documents may not be edited, what happens when one is overwritten anyway, the three ways folio points back instead, and why pointing back is worth the extra document. Old citations still land on the old record, and its banner points to the newer one an entry a report a project page cite R-12 banner: see R-13 R-12 as committed, status: superseded R-13 supersedes: R-12 names it; edits nothing The old result is never touched. The three citations still land on what they cited, and the banner, drawn by the engine from the newer result's field, sends every reader on. The ids are made up for the example. Step one Which documents are never edited A genre says how its documents change over time. Most are revised in place. A permanent record , such as a journal entry or a result, is never edited once committed. A frozen document, such as a locked protocol or a published report, is edited freely until it reaches its frozen state, and then never again except its status. The gate checks both against git history. Permanent a journal entry, a result first commit then never edited The gate compares the file with its first commit. It writes no status: its status is derived from what points back. Frozen a protocol, a report draft then locked then abandoned Edited freely until it reaches a frozen state. After that only its status moves, forward to one of its card's exits, in a commit that changes nothing else. Revised concepts, entries, maps, projects live then live then live Edited in place and always current. Corrections to these are ordinary edits, and git keeps the history. A protocol was locked yesterday and has a typo in its hypothesis. Can the agent fix it in place? No. Once locked, the file must match the commit that locked it. A new protocol names it in , or a correction entry about it says what was meant. Step two Overwrite against supersede, replayed Take one result that three pages cite. The measurement is redone and comes out different. Step through what each lane does, and what a reader who follows an old citation sees at the end. 1. Cited 2. Redone 3. Followed Overwrite edit the old record in place Cited. The result is committed, and an entry, a report and a project page cite it by id. Redone. Someone edits the result's number to the new value. The old value is gone from the page, and the gate fails the edit, because the file no longer matches its first commit. Followed. Had the edit got through, a reader who quoted the old value would follow the citation and find a different number, with nothing to say it changed or why. The three citing pages now point at a document that says something else. Supersede a new record that points back Cited. The result is committed, and an entry, a report and a project page cite it by id. Redone. A new result is committed with naming the old one. Nothing else is written: the engine derives the old result's status as . Followed. The reader lands on the old result exactly as it was cited, with a banner linking the new one. With the lab pack on, the gate warns on each revised page that still cites the old result, so the agent updates them. Both lanes start from the same file. Only the supersede lane leaves the library able to answer what was believed, when, and what replaced it. Step three Three ways to point back When a measurement is redone, the new result names the old one: . When nothing replaces a record, a journal entry does the pointing. Each row below is one instrument, and none of them edits the original. Instrument Written as Status of the original What the reader sees Supersede a newer record of the same genre, with , derived a banner linking the newer record; the old one keeps its id and address Retract a journal entry of kind , naming it in , derived the record stays readable, marked retracted, with a banner linking the entry that says why Correct a journal entry of kind , naming it in unchanged a banner on the document with the entry's text, saying what is true instead A frozen document keeps the status it was frozen with, and shows its corrections the same way. Where does a retracted result's status come from, since the result writes no status? It is derived: the engine finds the retraction entry whose names the result. Step four Why not just edit An edit erases the evidence that something was wrong. Anyone who read the old value has no way to learn it changed, and a page that quoted it now cites a document that says something else. A correction that points back keeps both, and the banner tells every later reader. The cost is one more document, and the gate makes sure nobody skips it. It is the same idea as one fact, one home , applied over time: the fact keeps one home, and its history is a chain of documents that point back.
title: How corrections work

description: Why each fact lives in exactly one document, and what the rest of the library does instead, for anyone writing in a library.
text: A fact lives in exactly one document, and every other document cites that one by id. A library kept this way can be corrected in one place, and a reader can always follow a claim to where it is held. Four steps make the case: what a fact's home is, what goes wrong when a fact is copied instead, how much of the rule a machine can check, and how documents about the same thing share it without sharing sentences. Three pages point at one home; none of them holds a copy the home holds the fact a guide chapter an entry a map row links cites by id Every arrow is a link, not a copy. Change the home and each page that points at it shows the change. Step one The rule A fact is a definition, a measured number or a decision. Its home is the document whose genre holds that kind of fact: a concept for a definition, a result for a number, a journal entry for a decision. Every other page links the home and says what the fact means for its own reader, in its own words. A definition lives in a concept Its holds the one sentence. Others link it with , and hovering shows the definition. A measured number lives in a result Its field holds the value, with its evidence and the command that re-derives it. Others cite the result by id in the sentence that uses the number. A decision lives in a journal entry One dated entry of kind , permanent once committed. Others link it, and the entry shows on every document it names in . A guide chapter needs the definition of a term that a concept already holds. What does the chapter do? It links the concept with , so hovering shows the definition. It does not write the definition again. Step two Why one home Two copies of a fact agree on the day they are written. Then one is revised and the other is not, and the library holds two answers with nothing to say which is right. With one home, a correction lands once and reaches every page that cites it. Below is one real decision in this library's history, and three pages that mention it. The pages are made up for the example. Pick a habit and see what the pages say after the decision. Restated in three pages Cited from one home The home: a journal entry The journal became one short Markdown file per entry, permanent once committed. Recorded as a decision: One journal entry per file . Restated in three pages a guide chapter Add your note to the journal file. stale an entry Each journal entry is its own file. revised a map row The log, one running document. stale Only the page someone remembered was revised. A reader now meets two answers and has no way to tell which is current. Cited from one home a guide chapter Record what you decided in the journal . current an entry The journal keeps the dated record of decisions. current a map row The journal , and why it is laid out as it is. current No page says how the journal is stored. Each links the journal concept, whose definition says it once, so the change happened in one place and none of the three was touched. The rule also makes a library checkable. A number that cites its result can be followed in one click to its evidence and the command that re-derives it, as R-1 shows for the time this library takes to check. Step three What is checked and what is judged Part of the rule is mechanical, and the gate checks it. The rest is judged by the agent, by reading. The gate checks No two concepts define the same term. With the lab pack on, a number shaped like a measurement cites a result in the same sentence. Every citation resolves to the document it names. The agent judges A paraphrase of a definition, written as if it were new. A decision restated as if this page made it. A number from another document, given as this page's own. Why does a concept's definition cite nothing? So it stays true when a number changes. Results are cited below the definition, never inside it. Step four Siblings share ids, never sentences A journal entry, a report and a paper about the same result each cite the result and reuse its figure. None is generated from another, because each has a different reader. What they share is the id, so they cannot disagree about the number. How corrections work follows what happens when that number turns out wrong. Three siblings, one result, one figure journal entry report paper the result its figure Solid lines cite the result by id; dashed lines reuse its figure. The three texts above share neither a sentence nor a generator.
title: One fact, one home

description: Why folio puts every fact the engine reads into metadata, and keeps the body as prose, for anyone writing or reviewing a library.
text: Every fact the engine needs to render, search, filter or check a document lives in its metadata, and the body is prose that nothing parses back out. That keeps the body free for the reader, and it lets the engine draw everything that follows from the facts instead of trusting a writer to keep a copy in step. The argument: a document has two places with two jobs; four readers take what they need from one of them; prose is no place for a fact a machine reads; and whatever follows from links is drawn, not written. Four readers take the facts from one metadata block; the body is for the person index.html genre title description status · tags reviewed body: prose the shell's header search the gate a map row the person reading Four machines read the same few fields, so each draws the same title and description. Only the person reads the body as prose. Step one Two places, two jobs A document has two places to put things. The metadata is a short list of named fields: in HTML, tags in the head; in Markdown, front matter. The body is what a person reads. Each place has one job, and nothing is written in both. Five fields are core to every document: a title, a one-line description, the genre , a status and tags. A genre adds a field only when the engine renders, filters or checks it, such as a result's number or a project's date. Anything else stays in the body as prose. A project page wants to say when its state was last confirmed. Body or metadata? Metadata: the field. The shell shows it in the header, and the gate warns when it grows old, so the engine reads it. Step two One file, four readers Because the facts sit in fields, the shell draws the header of every page: the title, the description as its subtitle, the status, the dates from git, and the tags. A body never starts with its own title. Search results, link previews and map rows reuse the same description, so a document is summed up once, by its author, in its genre's voice. Pick a reader to see which lines of the file it takes. The shell's header Search The gate A map row content/projects/attention-kernel/index.html genre project title Attention kernel description A tiled attention kernel for long sequences, checked against a reference implementation. status live tags kernels reviewed 2026-10-03 body The forward pass matches the reference implementation; the backward pass is not written. Next, write the backward pass. The shell's header Project Attention kernel A tiled attention kernel for long sequences, checked against a reference implementation. Reviewed 2026-10-03 kernels dates from git Genre, title, description, tags and the card's fields, in the card's order. The status is shown only when it is not . The created and updated dates come from git, not from the file. Search project Attention kernel A tiled attention kernel for long sequences, checked against a reference implementation. … the backward pass is not written … A search weighs the title, the description and the tags above the body's words, and ranks a draft lower. Each result is labelled with the genre, the title and the description, and the status when it is not . The body supplies only the words that matched, as they stand. The gate ok fields: title, description and genre are present ok location: the genre matches the folder ok status: is one of the card's states ok reviewed: a date, and recent enough for a live project ok broken-link: every link in the body resolves Each check reads a field with one spelling and one type. From the body it reads only what the machine must: links, which are citations, and the few parts a card names, such as a concept's definition. A map row project Attention kernel A tiled attention kernel for long sequences, checked against a reference implementation. The row's link text is the title from the catalog, so a renamed page reads right on every map. The shell adds the genre, and the status when it is not . Without a reason of its own, the row shows the description. Why does a document's body have no ? The shell draws the title from the metadata. A second copy in the body could drift from the first. Step three Why the body is never parsed A fact the engine has to dig out of prose is a fact a writer can phrase in a way the engine misses. Agents phrase things differently each time. A field has one spelling and one type, and the gate checks both. So the date in the header, the number on a result and the source a reading is about are read from fields, and are right or reported. Three sessions, three phrasings Last checked on the third of October. State as of 3 Oct, still accurate. Reviewed recently; nothing has changed. One field Missing or malformed: the gate names the file. Too old on a live project: the gate warns. Step four What follows from links is generated The same rule reaches past one document. Whatever follows from links is derived, never written. A hand-kept list of these goes stale the day after it is written. A generated one cannot. What it cites every link and id field in the document What cites it every link to it, from the backlinks index Journal entries about it every journal entry that names it in A guide's chapters its parts, in order A record's status for a permanent record , from what points back at it The rule that each fact is written once is argued in One fact, one home .
title: Why metadata comes first

description: By the end you have a library in your project, a few linked documents, and a way to review them.
text: How to read it In order, once. It is for someone who has a project and a coding agent, and wants the agent to keep a library of documents beside the code: notes, explanations, records of what was decided and measured. You need a git repository and an agent that can run commands in it. You do not need to learn the command: your agent runs it. Each chapter shows what to ask for, what the agent does in reply, and what you get.
title: Getting started

description: You leave with folio installed, a library in your project, and the gate passing.
text: Hand your agent the setup prompt folio is installed by your agent, not by you. Open your coding agent in the project where the library should live, and paste the setup prompt from SETUP.md . The prompt tells the agent to install the engine, confirm it runs, and then follow the set-up skill . The agent asks you at most three questions in one message: what the library is called and who reads it, where it should live, and which packs to switch on. Every question comes with a default, so "defaults" is a full answer. How many rounds of questions does set-up take? One. The agent asks everything it still needs in one message, and skips what you already said. Or install the engine yourself If you prefer to install the engine first, run , or . The command it installs is . Then ask your agent, in plain words, to set up folio here. It finds the set-up skill and carries on from the questions. Either way, you do not run again yourself. The skills call it, the way an agent calls git. What is the package called, and what is the command called? The package is ; the command it installs is . What set-up leaves behind Set-up makes a library in the folder you chose and commits it: It ends by running the gate , which passes on a new library, and by telling you in two lines what you can now ask for. Which file holds what the library is for, and who writes it? , the charter. Only the set-up and configure skills write it, and each change is recorded in the journal.
title: Install

description: You leave knowing how to ask for a document, what the agent does to write it, and where to read it.
text: Ask for a document in plain words Say what you want: "add a concept for eventual consistency", "write a note on why we pinned the parser", "log that we chose Postgres". The agent matches the request to a genre and confirms it in one line. It asks only when two genres fit equally well. The core has eight genres. A concept defines one term. A note states one idea with its reason. An entry argues a subject in sections. A guide, like this one, teaches in chapters. A map lists documents in reading order. A project page says where some work stands. A journal entry records an event. A paper is a LaTeX paper with a landing page. You want to pin down what a term means, so other pages can point to it. Which genre? A concept. It holds the definition once, and every other mention links to it. What the agent does to write it The agent follows the write skill. It reads the genre's card, searches the library so the fact does not get a second home, and creates the document from the genre's skeleton. It writes the title and a one-line description into the metadata, and the body in the genre's voice. It links every term that has a concept, cites other documents by id, and puts the new document on a map . Where it writes something its sources did not say, such as an example of its own, it leaves a flag on the passage for you to keep or change. Then it runs the gate and commits. The agent invented an example to make a concept clearer. How will you know? It leaves a flag on that passage, labelled "worked example". Flags wait for you on the rendered page. Read it Ask your agent to serve the library. It runs , and the library opens at . The home page shows the top-level maps and the latest journal entries. Every page has the same shell: the library on the left, with the maps and every document by genre, a header drawn from the metadata, light and dark themes, search on the / key, a preview when you hover a link, and a panel listing what the page cites and what cites it. Where does the list of pages that cite this one come from? The shell generates it from the links. Nobody writes it, so it cannot go stale.
title: Your first documents

description: You leave knowing how a library is structured by maps, and how to move, merge and retire documents without breaking links.
text: Maps are the structure A library's folders follow genres, so they do not tell a reader where to start. Maps do. Each map lists documents in the order to read them, under group headings, with an optional reason per row. The maps named in the charter as home maps appear on the home page as the library's topics. Every document except a journal entry must be on a map, or linked from a document that is. The gate reports any that are not. A page is on no map, but a page on a map links to it. Is it an orphan? No. A link from a document that is on a map makes it reachable, unless its genre requires a row of its own. Ask for the change, not the commands Say "tidy the maps", "rename this page", "merge these two", "this note grew, make it an entry", or "retire this into that". The agent follows the organise skill. It moves documents only through folio's own commands, so links are rewritten, comments and dates are kept, and a committed document keeps its id while its old address redirects to the new one. Why should the agent never move a page with a plain file move? A plain move breaks every link to the page and loses its comments. folio's move rewrites the links and keeps the comments, the id and the dates. Ask for a health pass From time to time, ask "is the library healthy?". The agent runs the gate, lists documents on no map, looks for thin documents and duplicates, finds drafts left for weeks and open comments, and reports what it changed and what is left for you. Structural choices, such as a new topic or retiring something you wrote, stay yours. Each reorganisation is recorded in the journal , so later you can see when a page moved and why. Who decides to add a new top-level map? You do. It is a change to the charter, made through the configure skill and recorded as a decision.
title: Organising

description: You leave knowing how to question a passage on the page, what the agent's flags mean, and how your comments get answered.
text: Question a passage on the page With the library served by , every page has a Comments button. Select a passage and ask about it: "is this still true?", "say why", "cut this". You can also comment on the whole page. There is no name to type: the server writes as you, your git user name. The comment is saved in a file beside the document and committed on its own. Nothing goes into the page itself. Where is a comment stored? In a file beside the document, , committed by the server. The exported site leaves these files out. Flags wait for you Some threads were opened by the agent. Where it wrote something its sources did not say, such as its own example or a claim from general knowledge, it left a flag labelled with the kind of addition. A flag asks nothing. It rests until you press one of its two buttons. Keep closes it, and the passage stays. Change asks what to change, and your answer becomes a question the agent picks up. You do not have to visit every page to find them. The Review page lists every question waiting on the agent and every flag resting for you, newest first, and the home page shows one line counting them. The agent left a flag on an example and you are happy with it. Does anything have to happen? No. A flag rests until you act on it. Press Keep when you want it off your Review page. Ask the agent to go through them Say "go through my comments". The agent follows the address skill: for each waiting question it edits the document, or declines with a reason, and replies on the thread saying exactly what it did. Nothing is deleted. Each thread shows its state in plain words: waiting, resting, or closed, with how it closed: changed, kept, declined or withdrawn. Once the agent's reply is committed, a changed thread also shows the passage before and after. If the document is a permanent record , the agent does not edit it. It adds a correction that points back, and the record shows it as a banner. The gate also fails while an open question quotes text that is no longer on its page, so a comment is never silently lost under an edit. You asked a question about a journal entry. Will the agent edit the entry? No. A journal entry is permanent. The agent writes a new entry of kind correction about it, which shows on it as a banner.
title: Reviewing comments

description: You leave knowing how to let others comment on a library served from a machine you share, and how each comment reaches git.
text: The server knows who is writing On your own machine, writes each comment as your git user name. On a machine others reach, the server cannot ask git: many people use it. It reads their name from the sign-in in front of it instead. Put the server behind a proxy that signs people in, and name the request header that proxy sets in : Ask your agent to set it; the configure skill changes the charter. Then start the server on an outside address: . Without the header in the charter, or on a request that lacks it, the panel shows the comments read-only and says why. A comment is never taken from someone the server cannot name. You run and forgot the charter setting. What happens when a reader comments? Nothing is saved. The panel says comments are read-only here, because the server cannot tell who is writing. Each comment is a commit Every new thread and every reply becomes one commit on the current branch. It holds only that page's comment file, its message is "Comment on" and the document's id, and its author is the commenter. Your own work in progress stays untouched, even what you have staged. On a deployed server, add . The server then pulls before it writes and pushes after it commits, so your copy of the library sees the comments with a plain . If the pull meets a conflict or the push fails, the server undoes its write, refuses the comment and shows the reader the error. The reader can send it again; nothing is half saved. The remote rejects a push while a reader comments. Where is the comment? Nowhere: the server rolled back its commit and its file change, and the reader saw the error. Nothing was lost in silence; the reader knows to try again. An exported site takes no comments writes plain files, with no server behind them. It leaves the comment files out, hides the Comments button and the Review page, and each page's panel says that comments are open where the library is served with . Publish the export for readers; serve the library for the people who review it. A reader of your exported site wants to ask about a passage. Where do they go? To the copy you serve with , signed in. The exported site shows no comments and takes none.
title: Comments on a deployed library

description: How to use folio, what its ideas mean, and the record of how it is built, kept with folio itself.
text: folio turns a coding agent into the librarian of a knowledge library that lives inside a project, or on its own. Every document has one genre , which fixes its job, its voice, its format and its checks. Documents link to each other, and maps give a reader the way in. You talk to your agent; it follows folio's seven skills and runs the gate before every commit. This documentation is itself a folio library. Every page you read here was written and checked the way yours would be. You ask In plain words, to the coding agent you already use. The command exists, but only the skills call it. The library is files Plain HTML and Markdown in a folder in git. Reading a page needs no build step. Nothing lands unchecked Every change passes before it is committed. The loop: ask, skill, write, check, commit, read, comment, answer You ask in plain words Your agent picks a skill It writes linked documents folio check the gate Committed to git fails: fix it and check again folio serve renders the site A reader leaves a comment address skill answers, edits the edit goes through the gate too read it saved beside the page, in git people: you, and readers the agent, following a skill the gate Follow the arrows from the top left. Nothing reaches git without passing the gate, and a reader's comment comes back in through a skill, so the answer is checked like any other change. Ask. "Add a concept for the gate", "file this paper", "tidy the maps". The agent picks the skill that covers it: set-up, configure, write, organise, address, run or publish. Write. The write skill picks the genre, writes in its voice, links the concepts it uses, flags what goes beyond its sources and puts the document on a map. Check. The gate reads every document: links resolve, maps list what they should, frozen records are unchanged, each genre's checks hold. Read and answer. The library renders as a site. A comment on a passage is saved in a file beside the page, and the address skill answers it on that page. New here? Start with the guide. It installs folio in a project and walks you to your first reviewed page. The cards above are the library's top-level maps: how to use it, its ideas, its specifications, and the record of how it is built. Getting started
title: folio

description: Documents carry five core fields, and the body is prose the engine never parses.
text: Every fact the engine renders, searches, filters or checks moved into metadata: title, description, genre, status, tags, and fields a genre declares only when the engine reads them. The shell now draws each page's header, and what follows from links is generated. The reasons are in Why metadata comes first .
title: Metadata holds every fact the engine reads

description: The journal became one short Markdown file per entry, permanent once committed.
text: Each entry is its own document under content/journal/, with a date, an optional kind and the ids it is about. Two agents writing at once never touch the same file, and every entry can be linked and searched on its own. See Journal .
title: One journal entry per file

description: A paper's source stays revised, and each frozen version is a permanent copy beside it.
text: A frozen paper could never be revised, so the model changed: main.tex is revised, and freezing copies the source and the built PDF into a permanent versions// folder. A later change is frozen as a new version. See Permanent record .
title: Paper versions are snapshots

description: The home page now shows a fourth map, How folio is built, so the lab records have a topic of their own.
text: home.maps was using-folio, concepts, reference; it is now using-folio, concepts, reference, building-folio. The protocol and the results about the gate's speed were reachable only through the question's fields, so no map listed them and a reader focusing the library on a topic could not reach them. The new map lists the project, the question, the protocol and the results. The source of the As We May Think reading joined Using folio for the same reason.
title: Added How folio is built as a home map

description: A comment has no name field, is one commit on the current branch, and is refused rather than taken anonymously.
text: The server knows who is writing: the git user locally, and on a deployed server the header a sign-in proxy sets, named in the charter as comments.identity_header. Each new thread or reply is one commit holding only that page's comment file. With folio serve --push the server pulls before and pushes after, and on any failure it rolls back and refuses the comment. An exported site takes no comments. Readers see waiting, resting and closed, a Review page, Keep and Change on flags, and what changed once a thread is addressed. The chapter Comments on a deployed library explains it.
title: Comments are committed by the server, as the commenter

description: The home page shows three maps: Using folio, Concepts and Reference, in that order.
text: home.maps was empty; it is now using-folio, concepts, reference. A newcomer starts with how to use folio, then the terms, then the specifications.
title: Home maps set

description: Vannevar Bush's 1945 essay, filed as a source with a reading, as the knowledge-base pack's worked example.
text: The source is filed with no identifier: its address in The Atlantic's archive could not be looked up from this session, and the source says so. The original is not kept: the article is public, and the source links it. The reading keeps to the memex and its trails, and is flagged for checking against the text.
title: Ingested As We May Think

description: folio's own documentation became a folio library in docs/, with both packs on.
text: Purpose: how to use folio, what its ideas mean, and the record of how it is built. Reader: someone deciding whether to use folio, or using it through their agent. Packs: knowledge-base and lab, so each has a worked example here. Location: docs/ in the folio repository, with root set to the repository so results can cite its scripts.
title: Library set up

description: The protocol timing folio check on two libraries is locked before any timed run.
text: Ten timed runs per arm, after one warm-up, with the gate passing on each. Decision rules D1 to D3 and predictions P1 and P2 are fixed from here.
title: Locked the check-time protocol

description: folio check took a median of 0.20 s on this documentation library.
text: Re-derived from the timings with the protocol's script. D1 holds and P1 is a hit; Q-1 is answered for the library at its present size.
title: Recorded R-1

description: folio check took a median of 0.21 s on the sample library.
text: Re-derived from the same timings file. P2 missed: the larger library was not the slower one.
title: Recorded R-2

description: The specs remain Markdown files in docs/spec/, linked from the Reference map by their GitHub addresses.
text: The specs are the contract the engine is tested against, edited with the code, and read on GitHub. Making them documents would give them a genre they do not fit. The Reference map lists each one with a reason to read it.
title: Specifications stay outside the library

description: The skills folio init installs point at the repository's own skills/ folder instead of a copy.
text: folio init copied the seven skills into .agents/skills/. In folio's own repository that copy would drift from skills/, the source the package ships, so .agents/skills is a link to skills/ and .claude/skills links to it as usual.
title: The library shares the repository's skills

description: The record of how folio is built and measured: the project, the questions it asks of itself, and what it found.
text: Current take folio is built with its own lab pack. Each question it asks of itself gets a locked protocol before anything is measured, and each measurement becomes a result. One question is answered so far: the gate is fast enough to run before every commit. The chain below is how that answer was reached, and every link in it is a document you can open. 1. Ask 2. Lock 3. Measure 4. Answer Question, locked protocol, two results, and the answer back on the question QUESTION Q-1 is the gate fast enough? PROTOCOL check-time locked before any run RESULT R-1 this library RESULT R-2 the sample never edited Q-1 answered the answer is written back on the question, citing both results Each box is one document, and each arrow is a field that names another one. The order matters: the protocol is frozen before the first timed run, so the decision rules could not be bent to fit the numbers. Ask. A question says why it matters, what would settle it, and what would make the library drop it, before any plan to measure. Lock. A protocol names the one variable, what is held fixed and the decision rules. Once locked, it is frozen: the gate checks it against git. Measure. Each run becomes a result: a number, its baseline, its bounds and the command that re-derives it. A result is a permanent record. Answer. The question's answer cites the results by id, and its status moves to answered. A later result can supersede one without editing it. The project folio Where folio stands, and what comes next. How fast is the gate Does folio check finish in under two seconds on this documentation library? The question: can the skills afford to run the gate before every commit? Time folio check on two libraries The locked protocol: what was measured, and what each outcome would mean. folio check took a median of 0.20 s on this documentation library folio check took a median of 0.21 s on the test suite's sample library Still open The answer holds for this library at its present size. The smaller sample library was no faster, so start-up likely dominates at this scale, and the question is worth asking again once the library is several times larger.
title: How folio is built

description: The ideas folio is built on, each defined once.
text: Eight terms carry the rest of this library. Read the library, genre and map first; the others make sense after them. Each term is defined once, on its own page. Every other page links to that page instead of defining the term again, and hovering the link shows the definition. The figure reads in tiers: what a library is made of, how the work on it is done, and how it keeps a record that can be trusted. The eight concepts in three tiers, joined by what each does Library Genre Map each document has one the reader's way in Skill Pack Gate changes it, step by step adds genres adds workflows runs it before every commit Journal Permanent record its entries are checks it against git Read down the tiers. The library tier is what you have, the work tier is what acts on it, and the record tier is what never changes behind your back. Start here What a library is made of, and how a reader finds a way in. Library Genre Map How the work is done Who changes the library, with what, and what stops a bad change. Skill Pack Gate The record Why the history can be trusted when a page cites it. Journal Permanent record Not defined yet Some terms the specs use still have no concept page of their own: the charter, a workflow, a flag. Until they do, the guide and the specifications are where they are explained.
title: Concepts

description: The specifications that define folio exactly, and what each one settles.
text: When a skill, a genre card or a page disagrees with the specifications, the specifications win, and the other is fixed. The specifications are the contract. The model comes first: every other spec builds on it and settles one part in detail. They are Markdown files in the repository, outside this library, so their rows link to GitHub. Come here with a question, not to read front to back. The table below says which file to open. The model at the centre, five specs around it, the shell beside them model.md the contract genre-format.md checks.md commands.md pack-format.md skill-format.md COMPONENTS.md Start at the centre. The five around it each settle one part of the model in detail; the shell's components sit below the line, about how pages are drawn rather than what they are. description: Varies the library checked, and measures the wall-clock time of folio check.
text: Hypothesis on this documentation library has a median wall-clock time under two seconds over ten runs. Intuition The gate reads every document once, resolves links against an in-memory catalog, and asks git about the few files with a lifecycle. A library of a few dozen documents should take about as long as starting Python and git. If it fails, the cost will come from reading git history or from rebuilding the indices to compare them. The one variable The library checked. Arms: , the small library the test suite uses (), and , this documentation library. Held fixed One machine, one Python, one engine version, both libraries in one working tree, run one after the other. One untimed warm-up run before each arm. The gate must pass on every timed run; a run that fails records nothing. Pinned configuration Allowed moves Nothing under test makes moves: the gate is fixed code and changes no file. Measures Wall-clock seconds per run of , from process start to exit, measured by with . Per arm, the median of ten runs. The script also records the number of documents the gate reports, to state the library's size beside the time. Decision rules D1: keep the hypothesis if the arm's median is under two seconds. D2: drop it if the arm's median is two seconds or more. D3 (kill): if any arm's slowest run is more than three times its fastest, the timings are too noisy on this machine; stop and find a quieter one before recording anything. Predictions P1: the arm's median is under two seconds. Confidence: 85%. P2: the arm's median is higher than the arm's. Confidence: 70%. What it cannot show How the time grows with library size beyond these two libraries, how it behaves on another machine or operating system, or how long the gate takes once the library has a long git history to read.
title: Time folio check on two libraries

description: Whether the skills can keep running the gate before every commit without anyone waiting on it.
text: Why it matters Every skill runs before it commits, and continuous integration runs it on every push. If the gate takes long enough to notice, agents and people start to skip it, and the promise that nothing reaches a reader unchecked goes with it. What would settle it The median wall-clock time of over repeated runs on this library, on one machine, against the two-second line. A median under it answers yes for this library at its present size; a median over it answers no. What would make us drop it Timings that swing so widely from run to run on one machine that a median says nothing, or a gate so fast on every library we have that the question stops mattering. Answer Yes, at its present size: the median was well under the line (). The smaller sample library was no faster (), so at this scale start-up likely dominates, and the question is worth asking again once the library is several times larger.
title: Does folio check finish in under two seconds on this documentation library?

description: The memex's trails are the closest ancestor of a folio map: a path through linked records, kept so someone else can follow it.
text: Items on one desk, joined by association, one run of joins kept as a trail, and the trail handed on ONE PERSON'S MEMEX a book a letter a record a book a letter a record 1 2 3 4 copied handed on ANOTHER READER'S MEMEX the same trail The essay's idea in one picture: the joins are many and loose, the trail is one ordered run through them, and it is the trail, not the pile, that is handed on. A link joins two items. A trail is a kept, ordered path through many, and it can travel to someone else. Items Joined A trail Handed on Items. One person's books, records and letters, all on one desk, any of them shown quickly. Joined. Items are joined by association, as the mind works, not filed in one place each. Any item can call up another. A trail. A run of joins, kept in order, can be followed again later. Handed on. The trail is copied and given to someone else, who adds it to their own memex. The essay says What it claims The record of what people know has outgrown the means of consulting it. The essay's opening argument. A device the essay names the memex, a desk that stores a person's books, records and letters, could hold everything that person consults and show any of it quickly. Where the memex is introduced. The memex would join items by association, as the mind does, rather than file each one in a single place: any item can call up another, and a run of such joins forms a trail that is kept and can be followed again. Where trails are described. A trail can be copied and handed to someone else, who adds it to their own memex. The same passage. My take What I make of it The trail is the part that has aged best. A link joins two items; a trail is an ordered path through many, made by someone for a reason, and handed on so a reader can follow the same path. That is close to what a map is in a folio library : rows in reading order, each with a reason to follow it. What the essay leaves to the person, folio leaves to a gate . A memex trail can point at an item that was later changed or lost, and nothing notices. In a library, a link that no longer resolves fails the gate, and a record that was wrong is corrected by a new one that points back, as How corrections work explains. A memex trail A folio map What it is An ordered run of joined items Rows in reading order How it travels Copied into another memex Committed, so every reader follows it When a target goes Nothing notices The gate fails In "As We May Think", what is a trail? A run of items joined one to the next in the memex, kept so it can be followed again and passed to someone else. In "As We May Think", how does the memex join items? By association: any item can call up another, and a run of such joins forms a trail. Still to check The claims are limited to the essay's best-known ideas, the memex and its trails, and were written from accounts of the essay rather than from a copy read for this page. Their locations are given by passage, not by page or section, until they are checked against the text.
